newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Eurofighter partner threatens pullout.
newsitem.headline: German Eurofighter partner threatens pullout.

text.p: Daimler-Benz Aerospace (Dasa), the German partner in the four-nation Eurofighter consortium, threatened on Wednesday to pull out of the project if Bonn continued to delay plans to buy 180 fighter jets.

But offering a glimpse of hope to the industry, a defence expert for Germany's opposition Social Democrats said he was confident Bonn would give the go-ahead to Eurofighter project despite internal wrangling over funding.
The head of the Eurofighter consortium in Germany, Aloysius Rauen, said that if Bonn continued to delay its decision on the project it would hit workers at all Dasa production plants concerned.
"If the political decision on Eurofighter is further delayed, the industry must start phasing out production," Rauen told a news conference.
The Eurofighter consortium comprises DASA, British Aerospace, Spain's CASA and Italy's Alenia.

But Walter Kolbow, defence policy spokesman for the German opposition Social Democrats (SPD), told BBC radio he had been assured by government ministers that Bonn would come up with an acceptable means of funding its share of the project.
"I think it will go ahead," Kolbow said. "They will have a solution to finance this aircraft."

German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said last month he was confident Bonn, under pressure to tighten budgets and qualify for European monetary union (EMU), would still find the funds needed to buy 180 Eurofighter jets to modernise its airforce.

Ruehe said he welcomed proposals by Finance Minister Theo Waigel to redirect state aid for the Airbus airliner to the four-nation Eurofighter project to help toward the planned 23 billion mark ($13.3 billion) purchase.
Rauen said Dasa was prepared to accept the plan, but wanted to be sure Bonn was going ahead with it.
After months of delay that have dogged the project, Waigel's proposals came as the latest sign the German Finance Ministry would at a pinch come up with the cash.

Ruehe has already offered to provide a billion marks from his own budget, which was severely scaled back last year, if Waigel comes up with another billion needed to assure that production of the jet can start.
He has said the final decision would come at the beginning of July when Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet are due to approve this year's budget which should include provisions for Eurofighter.
Ruehe was due to meet British Defence Minister George Robertson later on Wednesday for talks expected to cover Eurofighter.
Britain hopes Germany can overcome the problems which have hampered development of a project which holds the key to thousands of British jobs.

Eberhard Birke, business manager of Germany's BDLI Federal Aerospace Industry Association, warned the German government that the patience of other German companies involved in the Eurofighter project had run out.

"The industry is definitely no longer in a position to continue investing in a multi-million mark project using its own resources without the slightest assurance the programme will actually take place," Birke said. ($ = 1.731 German Marks)
